# Team of Teams: lessons for fleets and for people

<!-- practices:learn:start (generated by scripts/practices/practices.py; do not edit) -->
**Learn this:** [Visibility buys autonomy](https://github.com/evocaslab/hq/blob/main/practices/explainers/visibility-buys-autonomy/index.html) (explainer with a [quiz](https://github.com/evocaslab/hq/blob/main/practices/explainers/visibility-buys-autonomy/index.html#quiz)); [Hand-off latency](https://github.com/evocaslab/hq/blob/main/practices/explainers/handoff-latency/index.html) (explainer with a [quiz](https://github.com/evocaslab/hq/blob/main/practices/explainers/handoff-latency/index.html#quiz)). Learner path: Working with agents, step 4.
<!-- practices:learn:end -->

Source idea: General McChrystal's task force rebuilt itself from a hierarchy of isolated teams into a "team of teams": small autonomous teams that share context widely and
are held together by visibility, not by orders. The lessons below are project-neutral. Half (A) applies to a fleet of
agent sessions with a supervisor; half (B) applies to a human team and its manager. Each lesson has a cheap first try
and a measure. Read the evidence limits in [Sources](#sources) first: this is one practitioner memoir.

Page numbers are PDF pages of the book (see Sources). Related: [autonomous-sessions.md](autonomous-sessions.md),
[agent-workflow.md](agent-workflow.md), [research-flow.md](research-flow.md),
[measures-of-performance-and-effectiveness.md](measures-of-performance-and-effectiveness.md) (lesson B8).

## The core in two sentences

Autonomy is bought with visibility: "Eyes On, Hands Off" (p.219-221). And empowerment needs shared context first:
"empowerment without context will lead to havoc" (p.218-219). Everything else on this page follows from those two.

A fleet that checks every report against git already holds the first position: HQ's "reports are claims" rule is, by our
reading, consistent with the book's position, not a departure from it. But a hub-and-spoke fleet, where every session talks only to the supervisor, is what
the book calls the ceiling of a command of teams (p.131), so "we already do most of this" is too strong.

## A. For agent fleets

### 1. Autonomy is bought with visibility, and regained by the next verified report

Give each session a delegation level that the supervisor sets from the record, not from a feeling: for example
`land` (may land after the gate), `branch` (branch only, supervisor lands), `propose` (item or note only). A false
claim in a hand-back moves the session down one level; the next verified landing moves it up again. Tit for tat, no
grudge (p.187-188). Keep one bright line that no level crosses (the guard's never-list; privileged files stay
`propose`).

- Cheap first try: write the level in the ledger by hand for one round and apply it.
- Measure: supervisor turns per landed item, and reopened items or post-landing gate failures per level. Quality must
  not fall when levels rise; the book reports that pushed-down decisions were faster and better (p.217).
- Needs lesson 2 first: levels without a shared picture just move the errors.

### 2. Context before authority, and share the reasoning, not only the state

A session handed a decision without the picture around it will make a locally reasonable, globally wrong choice. The
leader's habit that fixes this is thinking out loud, so that thousands stop asking permission (p.173, 231-232).

- Cheap first try: a `decided <what>: <why>` line in the heartbeat or ledger; the start-of-turn brief shows the last
  ~20 lines: siblings' recent decisions with their reasons, answered questions, writers per repo, the plan pace and the
  flow version. Facts come from tools; a decision is labelled with its author and reason.
- Safety: everything every session reads, an injection reads too. Decisions in the brief are labelled text, never
  instructions.
- Measure: `asked` heartbeats and maintainer questions per landed item.

### 3. Siblings' lessons and findings reach siblings

A lesson saved to a practices page helps only the session that reads it. Put `Lessons saved:` and dated
`found <text>` lines into the same brief.

- Cheap first try: the supervisor copies the last three lessons into each new brief.
- Measure: hours from a practices landing to the first sibling applying it; stale-flow count.

### 4. Interfaces are where work dies

The book's point: work dies at the interfaces (p.129, 143-144). For a fleet: the hand-back, the landing and the next session's pickup.

- Cheap first try: log the time from "hand-back sent" to "landed" and from "landed" to the next dependent start.
- Measure: hand-off latency, not any session's speed. Speeding up the build while the landing queue stays still moves
  nothing.

### 5. Rhythm is a product

The book treats rhythm as a product (p.230), not overhead. For a fleet: a
regular supervisor round with an agreed shape.

- Cheap first try: a skipped round is logged with a reason.
- Measure: gaps over one hour in active hours, per day. Next to throughput, add an adaptability measure: time from a
  maintainer request to a session's first action.

### 6. Purpose first in every brief

State the purpose (why this repo or item matters) as the first line of a brief (p.107, 136). It never overrides
"Not in scope"; it lets the session choose well inside the scope.

- Cheap first try: one `purpose:` line per repo in the project registry, copied into briefs.
- Measure: scope incidents and questions per item.

### 7. Endorse in public, correct in private

Show good decisions in the shared round table; send corrections as direct messages (p.216, 231).

- Cheap first try: a `decided well` mark per session in the round table.
- Measure: share of sessions at the highest delegation level.

### 8. The leader is the limiting factor

When all decisions pass through one supervisor, the supervisor's turns cap the fleet.

- Cheap first try: count supervisor turns per landed item for a week.
- Measure: that number falling while quality (reopened items) stays flat.

## B. For human teams and managers

The same ideas, written for a team as it stands. Try one at a time for a month.

### 1. A short daily update with open reasoning (p.173, 231-232)

Ten minutes: each team says what it is doing and why; the leader says out loud why they decided as they did.

- First try: replace one status meeting with it.
- Measure: "asked permission" messages and decisions waiting for a manager.

### 2. Eyes on, hands off (p.219-221)

Visibility is the price of autonomy. A person who reports openly gets wider discretion; trust is rebuilt by the next
honest report, without grudge (p.187-188).

- First try: for one area, agree "you decide, I see everything after".
- Measure: manager-approved decisions per week, and rework.

### 3. Context before authority (p.218-219)

Never delegate a decision without the picture it sits in: the goal, the constraints, what the neighbours are doing.

- First try: before delegating, write three lines of context and send them with the task.
- Measure: how often the delegate asks "why" after starting.

### 4. The manager as gardener (p.221-234)

Spend time on rhythm, transparency and links between teams, not on individual decisions. Endorse in public, correct in
private. Visit with the questions sent ahead. Two questions from the book: "describe your very best source" (p.233) and
"if you were not going home until we win, what would you do differently?" (p.233).

- First try: one cross-team link per week set up on purpose.
- Measure: share of your calendar spent on individual decisions, falling.

### 5. Interfaces are where work dies (p.129, 143-144)

- First try: pick one hand-off between two teams and time it end to end.
- Measure: hand-off latency, not each team's speed.

### 6. Lateral bonds (p.192, 201-202)

Swap or embed people between teams for a while; trust cannot be ordered.
- First try: one two-week exchange.
- Measure: questions routed through a manager between those two teams.

### 7. Education for those who decide, rules for those who execute (p.157-158)

People who decide need the reasoning behind the rules; people who only execute need clear rules. Do not give everyone
both. A change of plan destroys prepared work (p.234); our advice: change plans rarely and say what of the old work survives.

- First try: write a one-page "why" for the rules your team follows most.
- Measure: exceptions requested per month.

### 8. Tempo is a means, not the goal

The book counts raids: about 10 a month, 18 by trying harder, 300 under the new structure (p.143, 221). Critics note that more raids were not a better strategy. Count tempo as a measure of performance (MOP), and keep a
separate measure of effectiveness (MOE): did the outcome you wanted happen? For a team: shipped items are tempo; used,
working, valued items are outcome.

- First try: add one outcome column next to your throughput count.
- Measure: both, side by side.

## Studied and not taken

| Option | Why not | Date | Reopen when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Push everything to everyone (a synchronous multi-hour briefing) | A capped, pulled brief with reasoning gets the context effect for a fraction of the attention; for agents, context size costs plan | 2026-11-08 | measured misses show a session lacked context the brief omitted |
| Embedded liaison sessions between repos | A second writer in another repo's lane; lateral information without lateral coordination is the substitute | 2026-11-08 | one-writer-per-repo rule is relaxed |
| Peer mesh (sessions coordinate directly) | Hub-and-spoke with a ledger keeps one place to verify; mesh multiplies unverified claims | 2026-11-08 | the supervisor measurably caps the fleet (lesson A8) |
| Trust without verification | The book agrees: visibility is the condition (p.219-221) | 2026-11-08 | never |
| An `moe` column in the round table | The Definition of Done already has "Outcome measured" | 2026-11-08 | DoD stops being enforced |

## Sources

Evidence level of the whole page: **weak to moderate**. It rests on one practitioner memoir; every number is the
authors' own, and the book says it is "not a scientific study" (p.17). An elite military unit is not a typical team.
The mapping to agents is our inference, not the book's.

1. Stanley McChrystal, Tantum Collins, David Silverman, Chris Fussell, *Team of Teams: New Rules of Engagement for a
   Complex World* (Portfolio/Penguin, 2015). PDF pages 22-253 read by a second Fable pass, 2026-11-08.
   Evidence: practitioner memoir, authors' own numbers (raids: p.143, 221). Notes, index and footnotes not read.
2. Findings and page citations: `docs/backlog/B-261108-team-of-teams-fleet.md` (branch `claude/tot-humans`), request
   R-2611081420-teamofteams, go-ahead R-2611081446-b811.
3. Pentland's and Axelrod's results (tit for tat, p.187-188) are secondary, via the book. Critiques
   (Hartung, Schake, Fastabend) were found in the first pass and not re-read against the book text.
4. Related HQ pages: [autonomous-sessions.md](autonomous-sessions.md), [agent-workflow.md](agent-workflow.md),
   [research-flow.md](research-flow.md).

Re-check age: years for the book's claims; months for the fleet mappings, which depend on HQ's tools.
